source: Chi, Feltovich, Glaser (1981) Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices (Cognitive Science 5:121-152)
finding: Founding study. Physics PhD students (experts) and students who had just finished one semester of mechanics (novices) sorted textbook mechanics problems by 'similarity of solution'. Experts grouped by the governing principle (energy conservation, Newton's second law). Novices grouped by surface objects named in the text (inclined plane, pulley, spring). Authors proposed that expert knowledge is organised in schemas keyed to principles, and that experts turn surface cues into principles.
numbers: 8 novices and 8 experts (count confirmed by replication papers we opened: a02, a05). Problem counts per experiment (about 24, 20, 20) are from memory.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened. Small samples; problems came from a Halliday and Resnick textbook; most original problems are lost (the lead author told Mason and Singh they were discarded).
agent_relevance: S0 gate should classify a problem by the principle or method it needs, not by its story. The first sort by surface is the novice failure to design against.

source: Mason and Singh (2011) Assessing expertise in introductory physics using categorization task (Phys Rev ST PER 7, 020110)
finding: Large replication with 3 introductory classes, 21 physics graduate students and 7 faculty. Introductory students were far less surface-bound than in Chi 1981, and calculus-based students overlapped heavily with graduate students on 'good' categories. Faculty sorted much better than graduate students. Authors conclude Chi's novice/expert split was too sharp.
numbers: Algebra-based classes N=109 and N=114, calculus-based N=180; 21 graduate students; 7 faculty; 25 mechanics problems; average 7.02 categories per student on version II; faculty rating agreement above 95%; mean share of problems in good categories 34.4% (calculus group) vs 18.7% (algebra group) on version I.
quote: suggest that there is a wide distribution of expertise in mechanics among introductory and graduate students
limits: Paper-and-pencil sort with written reasons (Chi used cards, no pencil). Students were enrolled in the course at test time; Chi's 8 volunteers may not have been. Only 7 original Chi problems were recovered. Chi's Study 2 (surface crossed with law) was not replicated because faculty disagreed about which principle is the elegant one.
agent_relevance: Expertise in sorting is graded, so an agent's classifier should output a ranked list of candidate principles, not one label. Faculty put one problem in several categories when two methods work.

source: Mason and Singh (2011) same study, Table 3: category-by-category comparison with Chi's 8 novices and 8 experts
finding: Chi's novices used surface categories heavily and never used some expert categories. Mason and Singh's students rarely chose the surface labels and often chose expert ones, even on the same 7 Chi problems.
numbers: Chi novices (n=8): angular motion 87.5%, springs 75%, inclined plane 50%, kinetic energy 50%, pulleys 37.5%. Chi experts (n=8): Newton's 2nd law 75%, energy principles 75%, angular motion 75%, circular motion 62.5%. Chi novices chose 0% of Newton 2nd law, energy, circular motion, linear kinematics. Algebra-based students on the 7 Chi problems: inclined plane 19%, pulleys 16%, Newton 2nd law 18%, energy 31%, circular motion 28%, linear kinematics 44%. Calculus group (version I): energy 73%, Newton 2nd law 38%.
limits: Different problem sets, so not a like-for-like test. The 7 Chi problems were harder to sort well than the new ones (within one SD). Chi percentages come from 8 people, so one person is 12.5 points.
agent_relevance: Surface-category use depends heavily on problem set and curriculum. A surface-versus-principle test for our agent must use a controlled problem set, not a natural one.

source: Mason and Singh (2010) conference version: Categorization of mechanics problems by students in large introductory physics courses, a comparison with the Chi study
finding: Short form of the same data. None of the 8 introductory students in Chi chose Newton's second law, energy principles, circular motion or linear kinematics, while 18% to 44% of the new students did even on the Chi problems. Gives a likely reason: Chi's volunteers may not have been enrolled in the course at the time.
numbers: Version II (7 Chi problems plus 18 others) was given to the 109-student algebra class only. In the long paper: ANOVA between the two algebra classes on 15 shared problems p=0.90; per-problem t-tests p from 0.42 to 0.96.
limits: Conference paper, thin statistics. Algebra-based students are likely worse than calculus-based, so the gap would grow had calculus students done the Chi problems.
agent_relevance: Replication results vary with how recently the sorter learned the principle: a model that has just seen the principle in context may sort by principle, one that has not may sort by surface.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) An empirical approach to interpreting card-sorting data (Phys Rev ST PER 8, 010124)
finding: Graph-theory re-analysis of a 50-card physics sort by 40+ sorters. Most variation between sorters was NOT expert versus novice. It was 'stacker' (few big categories, many multiple placements) versus 'spreader' (many small categories, few multiple placements). The expert-novice difference appeared only on the second principal component. This may explain frequent null results in card-sorting studies.
numbers: First two principal components explain about 87% of variability; PC1 tracks stacker/spreader, not expertise; expertise shows only in PC2. Macroscopic measures (number of categories, two-sample KS test on category counts) did not separate experts from novices. A 'Cognitive Categorization Model' fits a multiple-categorisation probability that depends on the number of categories.
quote: card-sorting experiments most strongly measure how individuals sort
limits: One course context (introductory mechanics); about 40 sorters. The authors say the finding is about measurement, not that Chi's effect is absent.
agent_relevance: If we use sort-based tests on an LLM, count-based summaries are weak. Compare problem pairs (which two problems are put together), not the number of piles.

source: Wolf et al. (2012) review of earlier card-sorting studies, including Veldhuis (1990)
finding: Veldhuis tried to verify Chi with three groups and four problem sets. Sets 1 and 2 (natural textbook problems) gave no clear conclusion. Sets 3 and 4, built so each problem had one principle and one surface feature, agreed with Chi for experts; novices showed 'more complex' behaviour. Telling experts from novices on surface features failed unless both kinds of feature were designed into the set.
numbers: Veldhuis: 94 introductory students, 5 intermediate students, 20 physics professors. Set 3 was a 4x4 matrix (springs, ramps, pulleys, plain terms by Newton II, energy, momentum, angular momentum). Set 4 was 2x2.
limits: Secondary report only (we did not open Veldhuis). The intermediate group was 5 people.
agent_relevance: Test items for our S0 gate must cross surface and principle on purpose (a matrix); otherwise the test measures nothing.

source: Wolf et al. (2012) review: Singh (2009) and Lin and Singh (2010) follow-ups
finding: Singh asked graduate-student TAs to sort twice, as themselves and as they thought their students would. Graduate students predicting students did better than real students (they overestimated them). Faculty did best, so graduate students are not clean 'experts'. Lin and Singh sorted quantum mechanics problems; even the faculty panel did not agree on every category.
numbers: Lin and Singh: 22 junior/senior physics majors vs 6 faculty; a 3-member faculty panel rated every category good, moderate or poor.
limits: Secondary report only. Small faculty group in the quantum study.
agent_relevance: Expert disagreement is real. A single gold 'deep structure' label per problem is a design choice; allow two valid principles when two methods work.

source: Mason and Singh (2011) think-aloud interviews and discussion
finding: Why students may choose surface labels even when they know the principle: they want to name specifics ('friction') because 'force' feels vague; some skip an expert category as redundant with one already made. Professors were more willing to use broad principle labels and often added a secondary surface category beside a primary principle category.
numbers: 4 introductory students interviewed with think-aloud, plus a few graduate students and professors. The gap in good-category share between faculty and graduate students was larger than between graduate students and the calculus group.
limits: Qualitative, 4 students. No rates.
agent_relevance: A surface label is not always failure to see the principle. The agent should keep surface tags as secondary index keys but route solving by the primary principle.

source: Mason and Singh (2016) Using categorization of problems as an instructional tool to help introductory students learn physics
finding: Summary of the same study with the proposal that group categorisation tasks can teach students to see deep similarity. Gives the ballerina and neutron-star example: both obey conservation of angular momentum, but students see them as unrelated.
numbers: Same samples as a02. 25 problems; instruction 'group by similarity of solution'. No new learning-gain data.
limits: Proposal paper; the teaching effect is not tested in this document.
agent_relevance: Training signal idea: contrastive pairs that share a principle but not a story, for memory retrieval keys.

source: Hardiman, Dufresne, Mestre (1989) The relation between problem categorization and problem solving among experts and novices (Memory and Cognition 17:627-638)
finding: Tested whether sorting quality tracks solving quality. Advanced novices (students who did well) sorted partly by principle, so the novice group was not uniform.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: Sorting by principle grows gradually; do not treat it as a switch.

source: Silver (1979, 1981) students' perceived relatedness of mathematical word problems (JRME)
finding: Maths version of the Chi finding: eighth-grade students sorted word problems by relatedness. Better problem solvers sorted more by mathematical structure, weaker ones by story content.
numbers: N and correlations not verified here.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: Direct support that the deep-structure effect holds in maths, our domain.

source: Schoenfeld and Herrmann (1982) Problem perception and knowledge structure in expert and novice mathematical problem solvers (JEP:LMC 8:484-494)
finding: Mathematics replication: mathematics professors (experts) sorted by deep structure; students (novices) by surface. After a problem-solving course the students' sorts moved toward deep structure, while a control group stayed surface-bound.
numbers: Exact N and percentages not verified here.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened. One of few studies showing the sorting shift can be taught.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the surface-to-structure shift is trainable, so a scaffold that names the structure first may work.

source: Chi, Glaser, Rees (1982) Expertise in problem solving, in Sternberg (ed.), Advances in the Psychology of Human Intelligence
finding: Review that sets out the expert-novice account: experts have more and better organised knowledge; experts spend relatively more time representing the problem and less calculating; novices pick equations by surface cues.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: Basis for putting effort into S1/S2 (understand, represent) before generate.

source: Larkin, McDermott, Simon, Simon (1980) Expert and novice performance in solving physics problems (Science 208:1335-1342)
finding: Experts work forward from givens using principle-based chunks; novices work backward by means-ends from the unknown, equation by equation. Production-system models reproduced both styles.
numbers: Speed difference not verified here.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: A computational model of what a schema does: it lets the solver go forward. A retrieved schema should supply the next step without search.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer (Cognitive Psychology 15:1-38)
finding: Schemas form when people compare two analogous cases; comparing two analogous stories raised transfer to the radiation problem more than reading one. This is a learning mechanism behind a deep-structure schema.
numbers: Transfer rates not verified here.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: Memory entries that store two or more solved cases with the shared principle written out should retrieve better than a single case.

source: Quilici and Mayer (1996) Role of examples in how students learn to categorize statistics word problems (J Educational Psychology 88:144-161)
finding: Students shown examples with different surface features but the same structure learned to sort by structure more than those shown examples with the same surface; surface similarity biased sorting.
numbers: Numbers not verified here.
limits: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked, search quota used up); recalled from memory. Treat as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: Vary the cover story across stored examples so retrieval cannot lean on surface.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Models were tested on 50 sets of GSM8K templates with only names or numbers changed. Accuracy varied across sets and fell when numbers changed, more with each added clause. Adding one irrelevant but plausible clause (GSM-NoOp) caused large drops. The authors read this as pattern matching to training problems, not formal reasoning.
numbers: Phi-3-mini fell over 65% on GSM-NoOp. Drops on GSM-NoOp (percentage points): o1-preview -17.5, o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o -32.0, GPT-4o-mini -40.0. Gemma2-9B worst-to-best gap across the 50 sets more than 12%. Giving 8 shots of the same question with the same extra clause stayed within the standard deviation, so no real help.
quote: models tend to convert statements to operations without truly understanding their meaning
limits: Not a card sort. 'Surface' here means irrelevant clauses and numbers; reading it as pattern matching is argued, not proved (a19 gives a more detailed account). Larger reasoning models resist better.
agent_relevance: LLMs show the novice failure: they read a distractor as an operation. Our S0 gate and S1 restatement should state what each sentence is for and drop unused data, with code checking that every number used is traceable.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (ICML)
finding: GSM-IC adds one irrelevant sentence to GSM8K problems. Accuracy dropped for every prompting method. Self-consistency over 20 samples helped a lot (the correct answer is among the samples for 99.7% of problems) but did not remove the effect. Telling the model to ignore irrelevant information helped, and so did putting distractor examples in the prompt.
numbers: code-davinci-002 chain-of-thought: micro accuracy 72.4%, macro accuracy (a base problem solved under all distractor types) 6.0%; least-to-most 77.5 micro, 18.0 macro. Self-consistency raised micro accuracy by over 11 points overall (35.5 on zero-shot CoT); best macro accuracy 45%. Fewer than 30% of base problems were solved consistently after adding distractors. Sentences with role overlap cut text-davinci-003 macro accuracy to 0 on problems of more than 2 steps.
quote: a single piece of irrelevant information can distract the models substantially
limits: 2022-2023 models, arithmetic only. Newer models are more robust, yet a17 shows reasoning models still losing 17 to 40 points on NoOp.
agent_relevance: Test items for the S0 gate: same problem with one irrelevant sentence that has role overlap. A good gate gives the same class with and without it; macro-style (all variants right) is the metric.

source: Qu and Gomes (2026) A four-stage decomposition of word-problem solving and mechanistic fragility in LLM math reasoning (EMNLP Findings)
finding: Inside Llama-3.3-70B, word-problem solving passes through four stages: Schema Abstraction (surface entities dropped), Operation Planning, Operand Binding, Computation. Entity names stop being decodable at layer 22, so the model does strip surface words. NoOp failures come from the Operation Planning stage, driven by attention heads that route through the distractor clause. Scaling those heads up recovers part of the lost accuracy.
numbers: Entity probe accuracy falls from 0.78 to chance (0.53) at layer 22; number tokens decodable (0.77) at layer 40; final answer 0.93 at layer 80. Llama-3.3-70B direct accuracy: GSM-Symbolic 0.241, NoOp 0.140 (-0.101), P1 0.068; with chain-of-thought 0.950, NoOp 0.780 (-0.171), P1 0.912. A global head scalar recovers 0.51 of NoOp failures. Digit-free filler had no effect (-0.004 direct); digit-bearing filler -0.067.
quote: NoOp fragility arises from the failure of a single stage in that pipeline
limits: One main model (70B) with two smaller replications; the NoOp set was re-created by the authors (original not released), with Claude Opus 4.7 proposing the clauses. Heads are model-specific. Preprint-level mechanistic claims.
agent_relevance: The model has a schema stage but fails when a distractor number looks like an operand. Digit-bearing distractors are the hard ones: code should flag numbers in the problem that the plan does not use.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in large language models (ICLR)
finding: Step-Back prompting first asks the model for the principles or concepts behind a question (for example 'what physics principle is involved?'), then reasons from them. It improved PaLM-2L on physics and chemistry multiple choice and other tasks. Error analysis shows principle errors (wrong abstraction) are rare; most failures come at the reasoning step.
numbers: MMLU physics: PaLM-2L 66.4% to 73.2% with step-back; GPT-4 69.4% to 84.5% (CoT 82.9%); Llama2-70B 51.9% to 64.8%. MMLU chemistry: PaLM-2L 70.9% to 81.8%; GPT-4 80.9% to 85.6%. Step-back fixes up to about 40% of base errors and introduces up to about 12% new errors. More than 90% of remaining errors are in the reasoning step.
limits: Principles are generated by the same model with few-shot examples; no sort test. With GPT-4 the gain over plain CoT is small (84.5 vs 82.9). Multiple-choice questions, not open maths.
agent_relevance: Closest working analogue of 'sort by deep structure first': one cheap call to name the principle before solving. Naming the principle is easy for the model; later steps fail. Keep it as a slot step in S1/S2 and test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with large language models (NeurIPS)
finding: An explicit schema store for LLMs. A problem distiller extracts the task and constraints, the system retrieves a high-level thought template from a meta-buffer, instantiates it for the problem, and a buffer manager adds new templates. Reported large gains on Game of 24, geometric shapes and Checkmate-in-One.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 3.0%, GPT-4+CoT 11.0%, ToT 74.0%, BoT 82.4%. MGSM average: GPT-4 84.4, BoT 89.2. Claims +11% on Game of 24, +20% on Geometric Shapes, +51% on Checkmate-in-One over previous best, at about 12% of the cost of multi-query methods. Disabling the problem distiller lowers accuracy, more on complex tasks (Game of 24, Checkmate) than simple ones (MGSM, word list sorting).
limits: Authors' own benchmarks, mostly puzzle tasks where the same structure recurs (template reuse is easy); the MGSM gain is small. GPT-4 and Llama3 only; not tested on novel structure. Ablation values are shown only in figures.
agent_relevance: A working schema library keyed by problem class. Supports memory keyed by deep structure; gains are largest where structure recurs, and G12 warns to use it only where there is a foothold.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant solved problems (and, for code, core knowledge) before solving. It beats 0-shot and few-shot chain-of-thought on average (+4%). The self-generated examples are tailored to the problem type, such as geometry or probability.
numbers: GSM8K (rows read from a partly garbled table, best reading): text-davinci-003 0-shot CoT 14.8%, 5-shot CoT 50.3%, self-generated exemplars 54.0%, with knowledge 61.0%; GPT3.5-turbo 75.0 / 75.8 / 76.7 / 77.8; PaLM2 60.8 / 78.2 / 80.7 / 81.7. MATH: GPT3.5-turbo 33.0 / 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3; PaLM2 27.1 / 29.8 / 34.3 / 34.8. K=5 exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH.
limits: Table text is garbled, so the row-to-number mapping is our best reading. Gains for the strongest model are small on GSM8K. Relevance of the self-generated problems is judged by the model itself.
agent_relevance: The model can name what a problem is like without a fixed library; useful when no stored schema matches. A check that generated examples differ in surface from the target would stop surface echoes.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat college students on text matrix reasoning and several analogy tasks new to it, but on story analogies it was weaker than students and, unlike them, did not reliably pick the correct far analogy (same causal structure, different surface). GPT-4 did better on far analogies.
numbers: Digit Matrices: humans N=40; GPT-3 above average human level, odds ratio 1.88 (p=0.005). Story analogies (N=54 students): humans clearly better, odds ratio 0.37 (p=0.0003); far analogy GPT-3 p=0.065 versus humans p=9.3e-23; 15 of 54 humans picked the analogous story on every trial.
limits: GPT-3-era result; GPT-4 tested only informally in the supplement. a24 shows the letter-string result is fragile.
agent_relevance: Choosing by shared causal structure over shared surface is the deep-structure sort; early models were weak at it, newer ones stronger. Test the actual model rather than assume.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-ran Webb's letter-string analogies on unusual alphabets (shuffled order, or non-letter symbols). Humans stayed high; GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped sharply. Reasoning that rests on similarity to training data fails when the surface changes but the rule stays.
numbers: Alphabets with n=0, 2, 5, 10, 20 permuted letters plus symbol alphabets; 420 GPT samples per alphabet and 40 for symbols; average human accuracy significantly higher than every GPT model across all alphabets and problem types (95% binomial CIs reported).
limits: Letter-string domain only; humans recruited online (Prolific). Prompt format picked by best performance, so GPT scores are an upper estimate for that format.
agent_relevance: A counterfactual surface swap is a cheap way to test whether our gate keys on structure. Use it as a held-out check (G3).

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) versus Qu and Gomes (2026): competing explanations of GSM-NoOp failure
finding: Two accounts. (1) Mirzadeh: pattern matching to seen problems, no formal reasoning. (2) Qu and Gomes: an orderly schema-then-operation pipeline exists and fails at one stage (operation planning) when a digit-bearing distractor draws attention. Their account cites a two-stage abstract-then-compute result (Cheng et al. 2025) that we did not open.
numbers: Qu and Gomes, Llama-3.3-70B direct prompting: digit-free filler -0.004, digit-bearing filler -0.067, NoOp -0.101. With chain-of-thought NoOp loses 0.171 while the digit-bearing filler loses 0.052.
limits: The mechanistic claim rests on one 70B model and constructed data. Both accounts agree that a plausible extra quantity is the trigger.
agent_relevance: The practical fix is the same under both accounts: code marks which given quantities the plan uses, and rejects plans that consume a quantity whose role was never stated.

source: Weak points and boundary conditions of Chi 1981 as shown by Wolf, Mason and Singh, Veldhuis
finding: From the papers we opened: tiny samples (8 and 8), volunteer novices who may have been out of the course, a lost problem set, graduate students used as experts when faculty do better, natural problem sets that confound surface and principle, and sort counts driven by a stacker/spreader trait.
numbers: Chi: 8 vs 8. Mason and Singh: 21 graduate students, 7 faculty, 403 introductory students (109+114+180) across 3 classes. Wolf: first two components 87% of variance, expertise only in PC2. Veldhuis designed sets 3 and 4 agree with Chi; natural sets 1 and 2 inconclusive.
limits: All of this is people sorting physics problems. The core claim (experts use principles, novices surface) survives in designed problem sets; the sharp two-group picture does not.
agent_relevance: Do not assume principle sorting is a binary property of the model. Measure it on a designed matrix set and report sorting style as a covariate.

source: Chi, Feltovich, Glaser (1981) Study 2 design as described by Mason and Singh (2011)
finding: Chi's Study 2 crossed surface features with physical law across 20 problems. Some problems can be solved by force or by energy, and the consulted expert solved them both ways; those were filed under the principle he judged simplest or most elegant. Mason and Singh note faculty do not agree on 'elegant'.
numbers: 20 problems in Chi's Study 2 (as quoted in the replication, citing p.131). Judkis, an engineering student, was the consulted expert.
limits: Second-hand description. Gold labels of the original rest on one person's judgment of elegance.
agent_relevance: Gold deep-structure labels are partly subjective. For the S0 gate test, use two labelers or accept two valid principles per item.
